224.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x & \text{for } 0\le x\le k\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

Trigonometric equations.reason: Must solve cos k = 0 on the domain to find k

parts.latex: Find $P(X\le 1)$. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k \sin x\,dx &= 1 \\ \Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^k &= 1 \\ -\cos k + \cos 0 &= 1 \\ \cos k &= 0 \\ k &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an equation involving a definite integral set equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \le 1) &= \int_0^1 \sin x\,dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^1 \\ &= -\cos 1 + 1 \\ &\approx 0.4597 \end{aligned}$$

136.stem:
People are given a maximum of six hours to complete a puzzle. The time spent on the puzzle, in hours, can be modelled using the continuous random variable $X$ which has probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}, & \text{for } 0\le x\le 6,\ (\text{where } A>0)\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}.$$

The graph of the probability density function is shown below. The graph has a local maximum.

\exfigure{222_q33_1}

figures.cap: graph of probability density function f(x) on 0 to 6 with a local maximum

parts.latex: Show that $A=\dfrac{2}{\ln 10}$.
Show that the mode of $X$ is two hours.
Show that $P(X<2)=\log_{10}2$.

The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores of people are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.

It has been observed that the puzzle is generally completed more quickly by people with a high IQ.

It is known that 80% of people with an IQ greater than 130 can complete the puzzle in less than two hours.

A person chosen at random can complete the puzzle in less than two hours.

What is the probability that this person has an IQ greater than 130? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

solutions.latex:
$$\int_0^6 \dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{A}{2}\left[\ln\left(x^2+4\right)\right]_0^6 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}(\ln 40 - \ln 4) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}\left(\ln\dfrac{40}{4}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}\ln 10 &= 1 \\ A &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 10} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the anti-derivative of $\dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{A\left(x^2+4\right) - Ax(2x)}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{Ax^2 + 4A - 2Ax^2}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{4A - Ax^2}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} = 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ 4A - Ax^2 &= 0 \\ Ax^2 &= 4A \\ x^2 &= 4 \\ x &= 2 \quad (x > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The mode of $X$ is 2.
criteria: Finds the correct derivative of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X < 2) &= \int_0^2 \dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}\left[\ln\left(x^2+4\right)\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}(\ln 8 - \ln 4) \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}\ln 2 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 10}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\ln 2 \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 10} \\ &= \log_{10} 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} &P(\text{IQ} > 130) \\ &= P\left(\dfrac{\text{IQ} - 100}{15} > \dfrac{130 - 100}{15}\right) \\ &= P(Z > 2) \\ &= 2.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} &P\left(\text{IQ} > 130 \;\middle|\; \text{Time to complete} < 2\right) \\ &= \dfrac{P\left(\text{IQ} > 130 \cap \text{Time to complete} < 2\right)}{P\left(\text{Time to complete} < 2\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2.5\%\times 80\%}{\log_{10} 2} \\ &= 0.06643\ldots \\ &= 0.066 \text{ (three decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to find the conditional probability, or equivalent merit

167.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases} 1 & x>e^3 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{k}\ln x & 1\le x\le e^3 \\[6pt] 0 & x<1 \end{cases}.$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=3$.
Given that $P(X<c)=2P(X>c)$, find the exact value of $c$.

solutions.latex:
We need $F\left(e^3\right) = 1$, since $F(x)$ is a CDF.
$$\begin{aligned} F\left(e^3\right) &= \dfrac{1}{k}\ln e^3 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{k} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{3}{k} = 1$.
$$\therefore\ k = 3$$

$$P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} P(X < c) &= 2\left[1 - P(X < c)\right] \\ 3P(X < c) &= 2 \\ P(X < c) &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(c) = \dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\ln c &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ \ln c &= 2 \\ c &= e^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises that $P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$, or equivalent merit

198.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by
$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 12x^2(1-x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}.$$

parts.latex: Find the mode of $X$.
Find the cumulative distribution function for the given probability density function.
Without calculating the median, show that the mode is greater than the median.

solutions.latex:
Mode of $X$ will be when $f(x)$ has a maximum.
$$f(x)=12x^2-12x^3,\qquad0\le x\le1$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=24x-36x^2\\&=12x(2-3x)\end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)=0$ when $x=0$ and when $2-3x=0$, $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Discard $x=0$ since $f(0)=0$, so the mode of $X$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
criteria: Finds the derivative of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x12t^2(1-t)\,dt\\&=\int_0^x\left(12t^2-12t^3\right)dt\\&=\left[4t^3-3t^4\right]_0^x\\&=4x^3-3x^4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses $F(x)$ as an integral of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$,
$$\begin{aligned}4x^3-3x^4&=4\times\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)-3\times\left(\dfrac{16}{81}\right)\\&=0.59\end{aligned}$$
The probability of the variable being less than $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is greater than 0.5, therefore the mode is greater than the median.
criteria: Substitutes the mode from part (a) into their cumulative distribution function, or equivalent merit

288.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right), & \text{for } 0\le x\le\pi \\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}.$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$.
Find the median of $X$, correct to two decimal places.

Cumulative distribution functions.reason: Sets F(t)=0.5; not_when says median from F(m)=0.5 also gets Median, i.e. both; kept when unsure

Trigonometric equations.reason: Must solve tan of a linear argument for t

solutions.latex:
Solve for $k$:

$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx&=1\\ 3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{\pi}&=1\\ 3k\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\ 3k\times\sqrt{3}&=1\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: States correct equation and attempts to solve for $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), solve for $t$: $$3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}=0.5,\text{ where }k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

$$\begin{aligned}3\times\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}&=0.5\\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)&=0.5\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)&=0.5\times\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t=3\tan^{-1}(0.5\times\sqrt{3})=2.14\text{ (correct to two decimal places)}$$
criteria: States correct equation attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A probability density function is given below: $$f(x)=\begin{cases} x-1, & 1\le x\le a \\ 0, & else\ where \end{cases}$$ Which one of the following, is the correct way to find the value of $'a'$?

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^a (x-1)\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_1^a &= 1 \\ \left(\dfrac{a^2}{2}-a\right)-\left(\dfrac12-1\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{a^2}{2}-a-\dfrac12 &= 0 \\ a^2-2a-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The roots are
$$a=1\pm\sqrt2$$
The domain is $1\le x\le a$, so $a>1$. The smaller root $1-\sqrt2$ is negative, so $a$ is the larger root, $a=1+\sqrt2$.

The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{x^2} & 2\le x\le 10\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ such that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
Find $P(X>8)$
Find the median of $X$.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{10}\dfrac{a}{x^2}\,dx&=1\\\int_2^{10}ax^{-2}\,dx&=1\\\Big[-ax^{-1}\Big]_2^{10}&=1\\\left[\dfrac{-a}{x}\right]_2^{10}&=1\\\dfrac{-a}{10}-\left(\dfrac{-a}{2}\right)&=1\\-a+5a&=10\\4a&=10\\a&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates $\dfrac{a}{x^2}$ with correct limits and equates to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $a=\dfrac{5}{2}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{2x^2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>8)&=\int_8^{10}\dfrac{5}{2x^2}\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-5}{2x}\right]_8^{10}\\&=\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 10}\right)-\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 8}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{16}\end{aligned}$$

The median $x$ satisfies $P(X\le x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^x\dfrac{5}{2t^2}\,dt&=0.5\\\left[-\dfrac{5}{2t}\right]_2^x&=0.5\\\left(-\dfrac{5}{2x}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{5}{2\times 2}\right)&=0.5\\\dfrac{-5}{2x}+\dfrac{5}{4}&=0.5\\-10+5x&=2x\\3x&=10\\x&=\dfrac{10}{3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly solves for $x$, or equivalent merit

717.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x\ \text{ for }\ 0\le x\le\pi.$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function.
Find the first quartile of the distribution.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\big[\cos t\big]_0^x\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x),\qquad 0\le x\le\pi$$
criteria: Finds the integral $-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The first quartile $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.25$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x)&=0.25\\ 1-\cos x&=0.5\\ \cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
The first quartile is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^2 x^2(2-x)\,dx&=1\\ k\left[\dfrac{2x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2&=1\\ \dfrac{4k}{3}&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The mode is where the probability density function is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}P(x)&=\dfrac{3}{4}x^2(2-x)\\ P'(x)&=3x-\dfrac{9}{4}x^2\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x\left(1-\dfrac{3}{4}x\right)&=0\\ x&=0\text{ or } x=\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}P''(x)&=3-\dfrac{9}{2}x\\ P''\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)&=-3<0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ is a maximum, and the mode is $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$.

1458.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{3x+1}} & 1\le x\le5\ (\text{where } A>0)\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that the value of $A$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
Given that $P(X<c)=3P(X>c)$, find the value of $c$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} A\int_1^5(3x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}\left[\sqrt{3x+1}\right]_1^5&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}(4-2)&=1\\ \dfrac{4A}{3}&=1\\ \therefore\ A&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up integral equation with some progress toward solving equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le5$, using $A=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_1^x\dfrac{3}{4}(3t+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{3t+1}\right]_1^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3x+1}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$P(X<c)=F(c)$ and $P(X>c)=1-F(c)$, so solve
$$\begin{aligned} F(c)&=3\big(1-F(c)\big)\\ F(c)&=3-3F(c)\\ 4F(c)&=3\\ F(c)&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3c+1}-1&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \sqrt{3c+1}&=\dfrac{7}{2}\\ 3c+1&=\dfrac{49}{4}\\ 3c&=\dfrac{45}{4}\\ \therefore\ c&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$

1069.stem:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}, & 0\le x\le 2\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.
Hence, or otherwise, show that the median of $X$ is $\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so $\displaystyle\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx=1$.

The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $5-x^2$, which is $-2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{-2}\int_0^2\dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{-2}\Big[\ln\left(5-x^2\right)\Big]_0^2&=1\\ k(\ln 1-\ln 5)&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k=\dfrac{-2}{-\ln 5}=\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$$

For $0\le x\le 2$, $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$; below $0$ no probability has accumulated and above $2$ all of it has:
$$F(x)=\begin{cases} 0, & x<0\\ p(x), & 0\le x\le 2\\ 1, & x>2 \end{cases}$$
where
$$\begin{aligned} p(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{kt}{5-t^2}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{k}{-2}\int_0^x\dfrac{-2t}{5-t^2}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{k}{-2}\Big[\ln\left(5-t^2\right)\Big]_0^x\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\Big(\ln\left(5-x^2\right)-\ln 5\Big)\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-x^2\right)+1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-x^2\right)+1$ for $0\le x\le 2$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median, $m$, is given by $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, where $0\le m\le 2$.

Method 1:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)+1&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5\\ &=\ln\sqrt{5}\\ 5-m^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ m^2&=5-\sqrt{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore m=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\quad(\text{since }0\le m\le 2)$$
Method 2: using $\ln\sqrt{5}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5$,
$$\begin{aligned} p\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)^2\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(5-\sqrt{5}\right)\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\sqrt{5}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the median is $\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$.
criteria: Sets $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ using the expression from part (b), or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{16}x^2\left(5-2\sqrt{x}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(5x^2-2x^{2.5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The pdf is $F'(x)$:

$$\begin{aligned} F''(x)=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10-7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)&=0\\ 7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=10\\ x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=\dfrac{10}{7.5}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\\ x&=\dfrac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Testing with the third derivative:
$$F'''(x)=\dfrac{1}{32}\left(-7.5x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$$

At an airport, luggage is weighed at check-in to ensure that it meets the airlines strict requirements.

They charge \$40 excess fee for every kilogram, or part thereof, a bag is over the 23kg.

$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^{30}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx&=1\\k\left[10x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4\right]_0^{30}&=1\\k\left[10(30)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(30^4)-0\right]&=1\\k(67500)&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\end{aligned}$$

No excess is paid if the bag weighs $23$ kg or less:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\le 23)&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\int_0^{23}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4\right]_0^{23}\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10(23)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(23)^4-0\right]\\&\approx 0.766\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

$\$200=5\times\$40$, so the bag is more than $27$ kg (up to the $30$ kg limit):
$$\begin{aligned}P(27<X\le 30)&=\int_{27}^{30}\dfrac{1}{67500}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10(30)^3-\dfrac{30^4}{4}-\left[10(27)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(27)^4\right]\right]\\&=0.0523\ldots\ (4\text{ sig fig})\end{aligned}$$

The waiting time in minutes, $t$, for a calculator check to take place before a student is allowed to enter the gymnasium to sit a mathematics task, has a probability density function given by

Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{324}$

What is the probability that a candidate must wait for more than 3 minutes for a calculator check to take place, given that they have already waited for 1 minute.

solutions.latex:
Since $f(t)$ is a PDF, the total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^6 f(t)\,dt&=1\\ k\int_0^6 \left(36t-t^3\right)dt&=1\\ k\left[18t^2-\dfrac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^6&=1\\ k\left(18(6)^2-\dfrac{6^4}{4}-0\right)&=1\\ 648k-324k&=1\\ 324k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{324}\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

The mode is where $f(t)$ is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}f(t)&=36kt-kt^3\\ &=\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\\ f'(t)&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $f'(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\\ \dfrac{3t^2}{324}&=\dfrac{1}{9}\\ t^2&=12\\ t&=\sqrt{12}\quad(t>0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(t)&=-\dfrac{6t}{324}\\ f''(2\sqrt{3})&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{27}\end{aligned}$$
$f''(2\sqrt{3})<0$, so there is a maximum at $t=2\sqrt{3}$.

$\therefore$ the mode is $2\sqrt{3}$ minutes.

The time in minutes taken for Claudia to score her first point in a tennis match can be represented by a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function given by:

1361.stem:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5 - x^2} & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$.

Show that the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ is given by:

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ 1 - \log_5(5 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 1 & x > 2 \end{cases}$$
Hence, or otherwise, show that the median is $\sqrt{5 - \sqrt{5}}$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx&=1\\ \int_0^2 \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\int_0^2 \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^2&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln|5-4|-\ln|5-0|\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln 1-\ln 5\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}(0-\ln 5)&=1\\ \dfrac{k\ln 5}{2}&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{2}{\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx=1$ with a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x \dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\left(\dfrac{x}{5-x^2}\right)dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\int_0^x \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\big[\ln|5|-\ln|5-x^2|\big]\\ &=1-\dfrac{\ln|5-x^2|}{\ln 5}\end{aligned}$$
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, and $5-x^2>0$ for $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=1-\log_5|5-x^2|\\ &=1-\log_5(5-x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Outside $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=0 &&\text{for } x<0\\ F(x)&=1 &&\text{for } x>2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral with a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-\log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ \log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ 5-x^2&=5^{0.5}\\ 5-x^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ x^2&=5-\sqrt{5}\\ x&=\pm\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$, since $0\le x\le 2$.

A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln 2)\sqrt{x^3}} & \text{for } k\le x\le 8\\[2ex] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\end{cases}$$

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^3}}=\dfrac{1}{x}$, the density is $\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}$, and
$$\int\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}\,dx=\dfrac{3}{2}\log_2x=\log_2\sqrt{x^3}$$
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_k^8\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln2)\sqrt{x^3}}\,dx&=1\\\left[\log_2\sqrt{x^3}\right]_k^8&=1\\\log_2\sqrt{8^3}-\log_2\sqrt{k^3}&=\log_22\\\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{8}{k}\right)^3}&=2\\\dfrac{8}{k}&=\sqrt[3]{4}\\k&=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt[3]{4}}=4\sqrt[3]{2}\end{aligned}$$

The median value is $4\sqrt[3]{4}\approx6.3496$.

1769.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}, & \text{for } 1\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$.
Find the median $m$.

solutions.latex:
Since $f(x)$ is a probability density function, the total area under it is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^5\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 &&(\text{the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, up to the factor }2) \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^5 &= 1 \\ k(\ln 26-\ln 2) &= 2 \\ k\ln 13 &= 2 &&(\text{log law}: \ln 26-\ln 2=\ln 13) \\ k &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 13} \end{aligned}$$

The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_1^m f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$, using $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{\ln 13}\int_1^m\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^m &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\left(\ln\left(m^2+1\right)-\ln 2\right) &= 0.5 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 13 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \ln 13^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ \dfrac{m^2+1}{2} &= \sqrt{13} \\ m^2+1 &= 2\sqrt{13} \\ m^2 &= 2\sqrt{13}-1 \\ m &= \sqrt{2\sqrt{13}-1} &&(1\le m\le 5,\text{ so the positive root}) \end{aligned}$$
So $m=2.492208\ldots$

$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}1-3^{-x} & \text{for }x\ge0\\ 0 & \text{for }x<0\end{cases}$$

The lengths of fish in metres in the harbour are distributed according to the equation,

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5 & \text{for } 0<x\le 1\\[4pt] -\dfrac{x-2}{2} & \text{for } 1<x<2\\[4pt] 0 & \text{for } x>2\end{cases}$$

People are only permitted to catch a fish whose length is between 0.45 m and $L$ m long. If 60\% of fish in the harbour are within this legal limit, find the value of $L$ correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The probability of a length between $0.45$ and $L$ is the area under $f$, so we need $\displaystyle\int_{0.45}^{L}f(x)\,dx=0.6$.

Total probability on $0<x\le1$: use the substitution $u=x^2-1$, $du=2x\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \big(-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5\big)dx &= \left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(0+0.5\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
Probability from $0.45$ to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{0.45}^1 f(x)\,dx &= 0.75-\int_0^{0.45} f(x)\,dx\\ &= 0.75-\left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^{0.45} \\ &= 0.75-0.37387\ldots \\ &= 0.37613\ldots \end{aligned}$$
This is less than $0.6$, so $L>1$ and we need a further $0.6-0.37613=0.22387$ from the second piece.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^L -\dfrac{x-2}{2}\,dx &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^L \\ &= L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4}&=0.22387 \\ L^2-4L+3.8955&=0 \\ L&=2\pm\sqrt{4-3.8955} \\ &=2\pm 0.3233 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1<L<2$, take the smaller root.
$$\therefore\ L\approx 1.68 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Forms and solves the quadratic in $L$, or equivalent merit

The time taken, $t$ minutes, for a machine to produce car parts can be modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function given by

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}k(t-1)^2, & 1\le t\le2\\[6pt] k\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right), & 2<t\le4\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Let $F(t)$ be the cumulative distribution function of $f(t)$, where $F(2.16)=0.3652$.

Find the least amount of time taken to produce 88% of the parts.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total area under the density function is 1.
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^2(t-1)^2\,dt+k\int_2^4\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(t-1)^3}{3}\right]_1^2+k\left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{1}{3}-0\right]+k\left[(8-4)-(4-1)\right] &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{3}k+k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4}{3}k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The first piece gives the probability up to $t=2$.
$$F(2)=\dfrac{1}{3}k=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25$$
Since $0.25<0.88$, the required time lies in the second piece, and we still need $0.88-0.25=0.63$. Call the time $x$.
$$\dfrac{3}{4}\displaystyle\int_2^x\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=0.63$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^x &= 0.84 \\ \left(2x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-(4-1) &= 0.84 \\ 0 &= \dfrac{1}{4}x^2-2x+3.84 \\ x^2-8x &= -15.36 \\ (x-4)^2 &= 0.64 \\ x-4 &= \pm0.8 \\ x &= 3.2 \text{ or } 4.8 \end{aligned}$$
$x=4.8$ is outside the domain $2<t\le4$, so $x=3.2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Time}=3.2\ \text{minutes}\ (3\text{ min }12\text{ s})$$

The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{6}{55}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function of $X$.
Find the value of $m$, correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1.
$$\displaystyle\int_0^1 kx\,dx + \int_1^3 kx^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 + \left[\dfrac{k}{3}x^3\right]_1^3 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2} + \left(9k - \dfrac{k}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{55}{6}k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k = \dfrac{6}{55}$$
criteria: Writes a valid equation involving the sum of all probabilities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0 \le x < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_0^x t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}t^2\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 \end{aligned}$$
For $1 \le x \le 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_1^x t^2\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}t^3\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 - \dfrac{2}{55} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 & \text{if } 0 \le x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 & \text{if } 1 \le x \le 3 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Describes the cumulative distribution function using an integral, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}m^3 &= 0.5 \\ 2 + 4m^3 &= 55 \\ m &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{53}{4}} \\ &\approx 2.37 \end{aligned}$$
The median is $m \approx 2.37$ (to 2 d.p.).

2631.stem:
A company manufactures light bulbs. The expected life of the light bulb $t$ in days is given by the probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}} & t\ge 0\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

A light bulb is considered faulty if its lifespan is less than 100 days.

Determine the percentage of light bulbs that are considered faulty and the $z$-score that 100 days would represent on a normal distribution curve.
Find the median number of days a light bulb lasts if it is produced by this company.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt&=1 \\ \left[-\dfrac{4\,000}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^\infty&=1 \\ -\dfrac{4\,000}{k}[0-1]&=1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k=4\,000$$

A bulb is faulty if its life is under $100$ days, using $k=4\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(0\le T\le100)&=\int_0^{100}\dfrac{1}{4\,000}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt \\ &=\left[-e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^{100} \\ &=1-e^{-\frac{1}{40}} \\ &\approx 0.0246 \\ &\approx 2.5\% \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ $2.5\%$ of bulbs last less than $100$ days and are considered faulty.

In a normal distribution, $95\%$ of scores lie within $2$ standard deviations of the mean. This leaves $5\%$ outside, so $2.5\%$ at each end.

$$\therefore\ 100 \text{ days is approximately a } z\text{-score of } -2$$
criteria: Finds either the probability or the $z$-score, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let the median be $x$, so the area from $0$ to $x$ is $0.5$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{4\,000}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt \\ &=\left[-e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^x \\ &=1-e^{-\frac{x}{4\,000}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} e^{-\frac{x}{4\,000}}&=0.5 \\ -\dfrac{x}{4\,000}&=\ln 0.5 \\ x&=-4\,000\ln 0.5 \\ &\approx 2\,772.55 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The median is } 2\,773 \text{ days}$$
criteria: Sets the integral equal to $0.5$ and makes some progress towards finding $x$, or equivalent merit

For a probability density function, the total area is $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k 3^x\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3}\right]_0^k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{3^k}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} &= 1 \\ 3^k &= \ln 3 + 1 \\ k &= \log_3(\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.67 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.67$$
criteria: Writes an equation involving a definite integral set equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The $8^{\text{th}}$ decile is the value $x$ with $F(x) = 0.8$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function.

$$F(x) = \int 3^x\,dx = \dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3} + C$$

Since $F(0) = 0$:

$$0 = \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + C, \quad \text{so } C = -\dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \le 0 \\[6pt] \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3}, & 0 \le x \le 0.67 \\[6pt] 1, & x > 0.67 \end{cases}$$

Solve $F(x) = 0.8$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3} &= 0.8 \\ 3^x &= 0.8\ln 3 + 1 \\ x &= \log_3(0.8\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.57 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the } 8^{\text{th}} \text{ decile is } 0.57$$

2841.stem:
A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(5-x), & \text{if } 0\leq x\leq 5\\ 0, & \text{if } x<0,\ x>5\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
Determine the mode of $f(x)$.
Find $P(X>3)$.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5kx(5-x)\,dx&=1 \\ k\int_0^5(5x-x^2)\,dx&=1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^5&=1 \\ k\times\dfrac{125}{6}&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{6}{125} \end{aligned}$$

The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest. Here $f(x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $x=0$ and $x=5$.

The vertex lies midway between the intercepts:
$$x=\dfrac{0+5}{2}=2.5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of } f(x) \text{ is } x=2.5$$

The probability that $X>3$ is the complement of $P(X\le 3)$, using $k=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>3) &= 1-P(X\le 3) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\displaystyle\int_0^3 (5x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5\times 3^2}{2}-\dfrac{3^3}{3}-0\right] \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\times\dfrac{27}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>3)=\dfrac{44}{125}$$

The total area under the density function is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 (a+bx)\,dx&=1\\ \left[ax+\dfrac{bx^2}{2}\right]_0^5&=1\\ \left(5a+\dfrac{25b}{2}\right)-0&=1\\ 10a+25b&=2\end{aligned}$$

The mean is $E(X)=\displaystyle\int x f(x)\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{35}{12}&=\int_0^5 x(a+bx)\,dx\\ &=\int_0^5 (ax+bx^2)\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{ax^2}{2}+\dfrac{bx^3}{3}\right]_0^5\\ &=\dfrac{25a}{2}+\dfrac{125b}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying by $12$:
$$150a+500b=35\qquad(1)$$

3060.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{9}\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 0\le x\le 3\\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{3} & 3<x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: In the space provided, sketch the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$
Hence, or otherwise, find the $75^{\text{th}}$ percentile of $X$.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

For $0\le x\le3$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{9}\int_0^x\left(t^2-2t+2\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{1}{9}\left[\dfrac{t^3}{3}-t^2+2t\right]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x\right)\end{aligned}$$
At the end of this section:
$$F(3)=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(9-9+6\right)=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
For $3<x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\dfrac{2}{3}+\int_3^x\dfrac{1}{3}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{x-3}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}x-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This is a straight line joining $\left(3,\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ to $(4,1)$.

Features of $F(x)$ for $0\le x\le3$:
$$F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(x^2-2x+2\right)$$
The discriminant $\Delta=4-8<0$, so $F'(x)>0$ and there are no turning points.
$$F''(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}(2x-2)$$
So $F''(x)=0$ when $x=1$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts4356_1}

The concavity changes at $x=1$, so there is a point of inflection at $\left(1,\dfrac{4}{27}\right)$.

The queuing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at a checkout in a store has the probability density function

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & \text{for } 0 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

By finding the expected wait time, determine whether the customer is more likely to wait less than 1 minute, or more than 1 minute.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is 1.
$$\int_0^4 kx(4 - x)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2kx^2 - \dfrac{kx^3}{3}\right]_0^4 &= 1 \\ 32k - \dfrac{64}{3}k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{32}{3}k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{32} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Integrate the density over $1 < x < 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(1 < X < 2) &= \int_1^2 \dfrac{3}{32}x(4 - x)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{3}{16}x^2 - \dfrac{1}{32}x^3\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3}{16}(2)^2 - \dfrac{1}{32}(2)^3\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{16} - \dfrac{1}{32}\right) \\ &= 0.34375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(1 < X < 2) = 0.34375$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the expression, or finds $P(X < 1)$ with correct reasoning, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $\dfrac{2}{16}(2)^2$ in the third line, an evident slip for $\dfrac{3}{16}(2)^2$; corrected to match the integrated expression. Final value 0.34375 is correct.

The expected wait time is 2 minutes, which is more than 1 minute.

$$\therefore\ \text{the customer is more likely to wait more than 1 minute}$$

3196.stem: A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.

solutions.latex:
A probability density function must satisfy $f(x)\ge0$ and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $1\le x\le2$, $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}>0$, and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 f(x)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{x}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -1+2 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Both conditions hold.

Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds and evaluates the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 2$, integrate the density from 1 to $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\dfrac{2}{t^2}\,dt \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{t}\right]_1^x \\ &= 2-\dfrac{2}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<1\\[6pt] 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right), & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$

The quartiles satisfy $F(Q_1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $F(Q_2)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $F(Q_3)=\dfrac{3}{4}$, using $F(x)=2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.

For $Q_1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_1}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= \dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_3}\right) &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3} &= \dfrac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The differences between consecutive terms are
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{Q_2}-\dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3}-\dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $-\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Hence $\dfrac{1}{Q_1},\dfrac{1}{Q_2},\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.

3231.stem:
A probability distribution is said to have a \textbf{memoryless property} if the probability of some future event occurring is not affected by the occurrence of past events.

In formal statistic terms, a random variable $X$ is said to follow a probability distribution with a memoryless property if for any $a, x \ge 0$ it is true that:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

You are given that $X$ is modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function of the form $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, for some constant $\lambda$.

parts.latex: Show that the corresponding cumulative distribution function is given by $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$.

Hence, prove the memoryless property for the distribution of $X$:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

solutions.latex:
For $x\ge 0$, the cumulative distribution function is the integral of the density.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \displaystyle\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt \\ &= \Big[-e^{-\lambda t}\Big]_0^x \\ &= -e^{-\lambda x}+e^{0} \\ &= 1-e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, and noting $X>x+a$ implies $X>a$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>x+a\mid X>a) &= \dfrac{P\big((X>x+a)\cap(X>a)\big)}{P(X>a)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} \end{aligned}$$
Using $P(X>t)=1-F(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda(x+a)}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda x}\cdot e^{-\lambda a}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
Also $P(X>x)=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right)=e^{-\lambda x}$.
$$\therefore\ P(X>x+a\mid X>a)=P(X>x)$$

solutions.latex:

For a PDF $f(x)$ with domain $a\le x\le b$, the CDF is
$$F(x)=P(X\le x)=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$$
Here the domain starts at $0$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \displaystyle\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt \\ &= \left[-e^{-\lambda t}\right]_0^x \\ &= -e^{-\lambda x}+1 \\ &= 1-e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. The median is 3. Find the values of $A$ and $B$.

solutions.latex:
The total area under the density is 1, and half the area lies below the median $3$.
$$\int_1^7(Ax+B)\,dx=1 \quad (1),\qquad \int_1^3(Ax+B)\,dx=\dfrac12 \quad (2)$$
Evaluating (1):
$$\left[\dfrac{Ax^2}{2}+Bx\right]_1^7=1,\quad\text{so}\quad 24A+6B=1 \quad (1)$$
Evaluating (2):
$$\left[\dfrac{Ax^2}{2}+Bx\right]_1^3=\dfrac12,\quad\text{so}\quad 4A+2B=\dfrac12 \quad (2)$$
Multiply (2) by 3:
$$12A+6B=\dfrac32 \quad (3)$$
Subtract (3) from (1):
$$12A=-\dfrac12,\quad\text{so}\quad A=-\dfrac{1}{24}$$
Then $B=\dfrac13$.
$$\therefore\ A=-\dfrac{1}{24},\quad B=\dfrac13$$
criteria: Creates correct simultaneous equations, or equivalent merit
Creates one correct integral, or equivalent merit

3660.stem: A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.

Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability must equal 1.
$$\int_0^2\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{a(1+4x)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^2&=1 \\ \dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt9-\dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt1&=1 \\ \dfrac{3a}{2}-\dfrac{a}{2}&=1 \\ a&=1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the total probability integral equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $a=1$, and using a second variable $t$ in the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x(1+4t)^{-\frac12}\,dt \\ &=\left[\dfrac{(1+4t)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4x}}{2}-\dfrac12 \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The complete cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right), & 0\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$

3738.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 4kx(2-x^2) & 0\le x\le 1\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.
Find the mode of the distribution to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\displaystyle \int_0^1 \left(8kx-4kx^3\right)dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[4kx^2-kx^4\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ 4k-k-(0-0) &= 1 \\ 3k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}x-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3$$
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2$$
The mode is the maximum of $f(x)$, so solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2 \\ 4x^2 &= \dfrac{8}{3} \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le x\le 1$, $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.

This is a maximum, as $f'(x)$ is a downward parabola, positive before and negative after $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}\approx 0.82 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Differentiates $f(x)$ and sets $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

$X$ is a continuous random variable whose probability density function is $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$ for $0\le x\le\sqrt{e-1}$ and zero otherwise.

Find the probability that $X<e-2$.

solutions.latex:
The probability is found by integrating the density over the values of $x$ where $f(x)<e-2$, namely $0\le x\le e-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{e-2}\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx&=\Big[\ln(x^2+1)\Big]_0^{e-2}\\ &=\ln\big((e-2)^2+1\big)-\ln 1\\ &=\ln(e^2-4e+5) \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is C.

A continuous probability density function is defined as $f(x)=1-e^{-x}$ for $0\le x\le t$ and zero otherwise. The graph of the function is shown below.

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$, and show, by substitution, that $t=1.84$, correct to 2 decimal places.
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right)$ and hence find the expected value, $E(x)$, of the function.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^t(1-e^{-x})\,dx&=1\\\Big[x+e^{-x}\Big]_0^t&=1\\t+e^{-t}-1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=x+e^{-x}-1$$
Substitute $t=1.84$:
$$1.84+e^{-1.84}-1=0.99881743\approx1$$
So the area under the curve is 1, correct to 2 decimal places.

Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right)&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}\\&=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
The expected value is $E(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{1.84}x\,f(x)\,dx$. Using the result above, $\displaystyle\int -xe^{-x}\,dx=xe^{-x}+e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(x)&=\int_0^{1.84}(x-xe^{-x})\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right]_0^{1.84}\\&=2.14384149-1\\&=1.14384149\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and progress toward the definite integral, or equivalent merit

3863.stem:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & 1 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: What is the value of $k$?
Find $F(t)$ the cumulative distribution function.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^4 (4kx-kx^2)\,dx &= 1 \\ k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] &= 1 \\ 9k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{9}$$
criteria: Provides correct equation stating that the integral equals one, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{9}$, the density is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
For $1\le t\le 4$, $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$, so the integral starts at 1.
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^t f(x)\,dx \\ &= \int_1^t \dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\int_1^t (4x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^t \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[\left(2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}-\dfrac{5}{3}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{27}(6t^2-t^3-5) \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{27}(6x^2-x^3-5) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Makes significant progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit
Provides correct integral, or equivalent merit

4043.stem:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$
After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?

solutions.latex:
The total probability over the domain is 1.
$$\int_1^{14} \dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^{14} \dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14} &= 1 \\ k\left(\ln 27 - \ln 1\right) &= 2 \\ k\ln 27 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$
criteria: Sets the total area equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $T$ days be the time at which the cumulative probability is 0.75.
$$\int_1^{T} \dfrac{\frac{2}{\ln 27}}{2t-1}\,dt = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 27}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{T} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \ln(2T-1) &= \dfrac{3\ln 27}{4} \\ 2T - 1 &= e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} \\ T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} + 1}{2} \\ &\approx 6.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 7 days}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to 0.75, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rounded up to 7 days since 6.4 days is not yet a full day with 75% chance.

4196.stem:
Mani is a fruit grower. After his oranges are picked, they are sorted by a machine, according to size. The distribution of the diameter, in centimetres, of oranges is modelled by a continuous random variable, $X$, with probability density function given below.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{3x^3}{4}+15x^2-99x+216 & 6\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{Otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ for the domain $6\le x\le 8$.
Hence or otherwise, find the probability that a randomly selected orange has a diameter greater than 7cm.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.latex: Find the mode of the distribution.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_6^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_6^x\left(-\dfrac{3t^3}{4}+15t^2-99t+216\right)dt\\&=\left[-\dfrac{3}{16}t^4+5t^3-\dfrac{99}{2}t^2+216t\right]_6^x\\&=-\dfrac{3}{16}x^4+5x^3-\dfrac{99}{2}x^2+216x-351\end{aligned}$$
criteria: States the integral for $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Corrected from source: the integrand and the antiderivative bracket had the $t^3$ and $t^4$ terms with a missing minus sign (written $+\dfrac{3t^3}{4}$ and $+\dfrac{3}{16}t^4$). The final $F(x)$ was already right and $F(6)=0$ checks.

solutions.latex:
The mode occurs at the global maximum, that is at a stationary point or at an end of the domain.

End points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f(8)=0$$
To find stationary points, differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(3x^2-40x+132\right)$$
Set $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-40x+132 &= 0 \\ (3x-22)(x-6) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=6$ or $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.

Values of $f$ at these points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f\left(\dfrac{22}{3}\right)=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The greatest value is $\dfrac{8}{9}$, at $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of the distribution is } \dfrac{22}{3}$$
criteria: Checks the end points, or finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

4283.stem:
$X$ is a continuous random variable that is defined by the probability density function,

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} k(x-1)^2 & 2 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{3}{26}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function.
Show that the upper quartile is approximately 3.74.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\int_2^4 k(x-1)^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k(4-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{k(2-1)^3}{3} &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{3}\left(3^3-1^3\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{26k}{3} &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{3}{26}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Sets the integral of the PDF equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is the integral of the PDF from the lower limit, with $k=\dfrac{3}{26}$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_2^x \dfrac{3}{26}(x-1)^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}\right]_2^x \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}-\dfrac{1}{26} \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integration of the PDF, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The upper quartile is the value of $x$ where the CDF equals $0.75$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.75 &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \\ 19.5 &= (x-1)^3-1 \\ 20.5 &= (x-1)^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x-1 &= \sqrt[3]{20.5} \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{20.5}+1 \\ &\approx 3.736851837 \\ &\approx 3.74 \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question

A particular continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{32}, & 0\le x\le 8\\[4pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

What is the median of this function?

solutions.latex:
The median $k$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^k f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\dfrac{x}{32}\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{64}\right]_0^k \\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{64} \end{aligned}$$
Setting this equal to $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k^2}{64}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ k^2&=32 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le k\le 8$, $k$ is positive, so $k=4\sqrt{2}$.

Hence the answer is option D.

Show that the function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right),\ [0,6]$$

is a probability density function.
For a particular continuous random variable $X$, find $P(X\le 4)$ for the function described in part (a)

solutions.latex:
A probability density function needs $f(x)\ge0$ on the domain and a total area of $1$.

For $0\le x\le6$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\le\pi$, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\ge0$ (see graph). Hence $f(x)\ge0$.

\exfigure{1307_q16a_s1}

Now find the total area:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)dx&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\right]_0^6\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\pi+\dfrac6\pi\cos0\right]\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left(-\dfrac6\pi\times(-1)+\dfrac6\pi\times1\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\dfrac{12}{\pi}\\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the function is a probability density function, since }f(x)\ge0\text{ and }\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=1.$$

4718.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right) & 0 \le x \le 1 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
Find $P\left(X < \dfrac{1}{2} \mid X < \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$
Find the median of $X$.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\left[\dfrac{2}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right]_0^1 &= 1\\ \dfrac{2k}{\pi}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin 0\right) &= 1\\ k &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: States the correct integral equality involving $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $P(X \le m) = 0.5$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^m \dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)dx &= 0.5\\ \left[\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)\right]_0^m &= 0.5\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi m}{2}\right) &= 0.5\end{aligned}$$

Since $0 \le m \le 1$, we have $\dfrac{\pi m}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\therefore\ m = \dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Finds the correct trigonometric equation, or solves an incorrect trigonometric integral equated to $0.5$, or equivalent merit
States the correct integral equation involving the median variable, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{2}\right)dt=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)$ for $0\le x\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(X<\dfrac12 \,\middle|\, X<\dfrac23\right) &= \dfrac{P\left(X<\frac12\right)}{P\left(X<\frac23\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{4}}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}\ (\approx0.816) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the conditional probability formula, or equivalent merit

4634.stem:
A continuous random variable $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$.
After how many days will a person have a $75\%$ chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^{14}\dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt&=1\\\dfrac{1}{2}k\int_1^{14}\dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt&=1\\\dfrac{1}{2}k\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14}&=1\\\dfrac{1}{2}k(\ln27-\ln1)&=1\\\dfrac{1}{2}k\ln27&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{2}{\ln27}$$

The probability of showing symptoms by day $t$ is $0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^t\dfrac{k}{2u-1}\,du&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{2}k\Big[\ln(2u-1)\Big]_1^t&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{\ln27}\ln(2t-1)&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\ln(2t-1)&=\dfrac{3\ln27}{4}\\2t-1&=e^{\frac{3\ln27}{4}}\\t&=6.422\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after approximately } 6.4 \text{ days}$$

parts.latex:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function, where $k>0$.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\cos 2x & \text{for } -k\le x\le k\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

Which of the following is true?
can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The density is $f(x)=\cos 2x$ on $-k\le x\le k$. Since $\cos(-2x)=\cos 2x$, $f$ is an even function, so its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

The area to the right of $x=0.2$ therefore equals the area to the left of $x=-0.2$:
$$P(X>0.2)=P(X<-0.2)$$
Option B is false because $1-P(X<-0.2)=P(X\ge -0.2)$, which includes the large central area as well as the right tail, so it is greater than $P(X>0.2)$.

Option C is false because $P(-0.2<X<0.2)$ includes the large central area near $x=0$. Option D is false because $P(0<X<0.2)$ is the area between $0$ and $0.2$, where $\cos 2x$ is close to its maximum, not the tail.

meta.self_check: Even function symmetry; B now 1-P(X<-0.2)=P(X>=-0.2), larger than P(X>0.2), so only A is true.

4788.stem:
Consider the probability density function for a random variable $X$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}} & 0 \le x \le 9 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ and hence write the equation of the Cumulative Density Function.
Find the median value of $X$.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is 1:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^9\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{3\times\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^9&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[(9+27)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[6-3\right]&=1 \\ 2k&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^x(9+3t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{(9+3t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}\times 3}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{3}(9)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2},\qquad F(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 9$$
criteria: Correct value of $k$, or equivalent merit
Sets the integral equal to 1 and integrates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3m}-1&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{9+3m}&=\dfrac{9}{2} \\ 9+3m&=\dfrac{81}{4} \\ 3m&=\dfrac{45}{4} \\ m&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{median}=\dfrac{15}{4}$$
criteria: Realises the median is found by setting $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: triangular pdf graph, peak 0.5 at x=2, zero at x=4

solutions.latex:
The area under the triangle is
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}bh=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 0.5=1\text{ unit}^2$$
So $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=1$, and $f(x)=0$ outside $(0,4)$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$. Also $f(x)\ge 0$, so it could be a probability density function.

For $0\le x<2$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{0.5}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the $y$-intercept is $0$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{4}$.

For $2\le x\le 4$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{-0.5}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}$, and $y=0$ when $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-\dfrac{1}{4}(x-4) \\ y&=1-\dfrac{x}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{4} & 0\le x<2\\[6pt] 1-\dfrac{x}{4} & 2\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
criteria: Finds the two equations, or equivalent merit
Any reasonable explanation about area $=1\text{ unit}^2$

4893.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} & \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function
Find $P(1.6 \le X \le 2)$
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x f(t)\,dt$ for $1\le x\le 2$.

$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\left(\dfrac{t}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{4}+\dfrac{t}{4}\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} \end{aligned}$$

For $x<1$, $F(x)=0$, and for $x>2$, $F(x)=1$.

$$\therefore\ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x<1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} & 1\le x\le 2 \\[6pt] 1 & x>2 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Integrates $f(x)$ from $1$ to $x$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave $F(x)=0$ otherwise; we wrote the cases $0$ for $x<1$ and $1$ for $x>2$ (standard CDF), which is the meaning of 'otherwise'. Used dummy variable $t$ in the integral (source reused $x$). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(1.6\le X\le 2) &= F(2)-F(1.6) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2^2}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1.6^2}{4}+\dfrac{1.6}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 0.46 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(1.6\le X\le 2)=0.46 \left(=\dfrac{23}{50}\right)$$

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ represents probability density function.
Find the mode of the probability density function $f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is a probability density function if $f(x)\ge0$ on its domain and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $0\le x\le1$, $6x(1-x)\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1(6x-6x^2)\,dx&=\left[3x^2-2x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &=(3-2)-0 \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest.

Since $f(x)=6x(1-x)$ is a concave-down parabola with zeros at $0$ and $1$, its maximum lies midway between them.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=x=\dfrac12$$

5025.stem:
Given the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}2e^{-2x} & x\ge 0\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
Hence find the median.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x 2e^{-2x}\,dx \\ &= 2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\Big[e^{-2x}\Big]_0^x \\ &= -\left[e^{-2x}-e^0\right] \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=1-e^{-2x}\quad (x\ge 0)$$

Let $m$ be the median, so $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2} &= 1-e^{-2m} \\ e^{-2m} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ -2m &= \ln\dfrac{1}{2} \\ m &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\ (=\ln\sqrt{2}\approx 0.347)$$
criteria: Equates $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and shows significant progress to find the value of the median, or equivalent merit

5056.stem:
The length of time, in minutes, that a customer queues to buy toilet paper is a random variable, $X$, with probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k(64-x^2) & \text{for } 0\le x\le 8\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{1024}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function.
Find the probability that a customer will queue for longer than $5$ minutes, round your answer to $4$ significant figures.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$, so
$$\int_0^8 k(64-x^2)\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[64x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^8 &= 1 \\ k\left[64\times8-\dfrac{8^3}{3}-0\right] &= 1 \\ k\times\dfrac{1024}{3} &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{1024} \end{aligned}$$

The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for $0\le x\le 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x \dfrac{3}{1024}(64-t^2)\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{1024}\left[64t-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{1024}\left(64x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3x}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{1024} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac{3x}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{1024} & 0\le x\le8\\[6pt] 1 & x>8\end{cases}$$

meta.format_note: Source used $x$ as both the limit and the dummy variable; changed the dummy variable to $t$ (notation only).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>5) &= 1-P(X\le5) \\ &= 1-F(5) \\ &= 1-\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\times5-\dfrac{5^3}{1024}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{189}{1024} \\ &= 0.184570\dots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>5)\approx0.1846 \text{ (4 significant figures)}$$

5089.stem:
The time $t$ minutes that a customer spends waiting in a queue has a probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x(k-x)}{36} & \text{for } 0\le x\le k\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: symmetric pdf curve on [0,6] with axis of symmetry at x = 3

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 6.
Write down the value of $E(X)$.
Calculate $\text{Var}(X)$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so $\displaystyle\int_0^k f(x)\,dx=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{36}\int_0^k(kx-x^2)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{kx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{k^3}{2}-\dfrac{k^3}{3}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{3k^3-2k^3}{6}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{k^3}{216} \end{aligned}$$

5133.stem: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distributive function (CDF)

The CDF is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos t\right]_0^x \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x) \end{aligned}$$

The first quartile satisfies $F(x)=0.25$.

5279.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Where $k$ is a constant

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{12}$
Fully define the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
Show that the median of $X$ lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^4\left(x^2-2x+2\right)dx=1$$
$$k\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x\right]_1^4=1$$
$$k\left(\left(\dfrac{64}{3}-16+8\right)-\left(\dfrac13-1+2\right)\right)=1$$
$$12k=1$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{12}$$
criteria: Correct antiderivative or set-up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{12}\displaystyle\int_1^x\left(t^2-2t+2\right)dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12}\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x-\dfrac43\right] \\ &=\dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 & 1\le x\le4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Correct middle expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.2)&=\dfrac{3.2^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.2^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.2}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.479 \\ &<0.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.3)&=\dfrac{3.3^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.3^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.3}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.5296 \\ &>0.5 \end{aligned}$$
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$, and $F$ is increasing.

$\therefore$ the median lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$.

5341.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a function $f$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x^3 - x + a, & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ which makes $f(x)$ a valid probability density function
Find the expected value and variance of $X$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1 and $f(x) = 0$ elsewhere, so
$$\int_0^1 (2x^3 - x + a)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{x^4}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + ax\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} + a &= 1 \\ a &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the integral equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Expected value:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) = \mu &= \int_0^1 x(2x^3 - x + 1)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^4 - x^2 + x)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{5}x^5 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{17}{30} \end{aligned}$$
Variance:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 &= \int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx - \mu^2 \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^5 - x^3 + x^2)\,dx - \left(\dfrac{17}{30}\right)^2 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^6 - \dfrac{1}{4}x^4 + \dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^1 - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{375}{900} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{86}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{43}{450} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expected value and variance formula, or equivalent merit
Writes the integral for $E(X)$, or equivalent merit

5421.stem:
Consider the probability density function $f$ for a random variable $X$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}; & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 0; & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $a$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Find the value of $a$.
Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.
Hence find the interquartile range, $Q_3-Q_1$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$1=\int_0^8\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=a\int_0^8(9+2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &=a\Big[(9+2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big]_0^8 \\ &=a(5-3) \\ &=2a \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^x(9+2t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\sqrt{9+2t}\Big]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{9+2x}-3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\[1ex] \dfrac{\sqrt{9+2x}-3}{2} & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 1 & x>8\end{cases}$$

Make $x$ the subject of $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{9+2x}-\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$x=\dfrac{\left[2\left(\frac{3}{2}+F(x)\right)\right]^2-9}{2}$$
$Q_3$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$Q_3=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{45}{8}=5.625$$
$Q_1$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$Q_1=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{13}{8}=1.625$$
$$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=4$$
criteria: Finds $x$ in terms of $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

5447.stem:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at the checkout of a supermarket has the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x) & 0\le x\le k\\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 5.
Is a customer more likely to wait less than 3 minutes, or more than 3 minutes? Justify your answer with calculations.

solutions.latex:
Total probability is 1.
$$\int_0^k \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x)\,dx=1$$
$$\dfrac{12}{625}\int_0^k (kx^2-x^3)\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{kx^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^k=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{3}-\dfrac{k^4}{4}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{12}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
So $k^4=625$, and since $k\ge 0$,
$$\therefore\ k=5$$
criteria: Correctly integrates between $0$ and $k$ and sets the result equal to $1$, or equivalent merit
Sets up a correct integral equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the probability of waiting at least 3 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 3) &= \int_3^5 \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(5-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\int_3^5 (5x^2-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{5x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_3^5 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\left(\dfrac{625}{3}-\dfrac{625}{4}\right)-\left(45-\dfrac{81}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{625}{12}-\dfrac{99}{4}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{328}{625} \\ &= 0.5248 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5248>0.5$, a customer is more likely to wait more than 3 minutes.
criteria: Correctly integrates between appropriate bounds and finds a probability but does not interpret it, or equivalent merit

5616.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function $F$ given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for } x<1,\\ k(x^2-x) & \text{for } 1\leq x\leq 2,\\ 1 & \text{for } x>2,\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{2}$, and hence find the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile value of $X$, giving your answer correct to three significant figures.
Find an expression for $f(x)$ which represents the probability density function of $X$.

solutions.latex:
Since $F$ is continuous and $F(x)=1$ for $x>2$, $F(2)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=k(2^2-2)\\ 1&=2k\\ k&=\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
For the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile, solve $F(x)=0.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.9&=\dfrac12(x^2-x)\\ 1.8&=x^2-x\\ 0&=x^2-x-1.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4\times1\times(-1.8)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{8.2}}{2}\\ &=1.932,\ -0.932\end{aligned}$$
Since $1\le x\le2$, we take the positive root.
$$\therefore\ x=1.93 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$
criteria: Shows $k=\dfrac12$ and sets up the quadratic, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave 1.932 (3 d.p.) though the question asks for 3 significant figures; corrected to 1.93 (3 s.f.). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The density function is the derivative of $F$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=F'(x)\\ &=\dfrac12(2x-1)\\ &=x-\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\begin{cases}x-\dfrac12 & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

5669.stem:
The monthly sales, $X$ (in units of \$100, 000), of a business are modelled by the two probability density functions:

$$g(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 1}$$

OR

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^3(1 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 2}$$

parts.latex: Determine the value of $k$ in the second model.
Show that the two models have the same median value.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is $1$:
$$k\int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx=1$$
Evaluate the integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^6}{6}\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{k}{12}=1$, giving
$$k=12$$

Let $M$ be the median of model $g$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}&=\int_0^M 2x\,dx \\ &=\Big[x^2\Big]_0^M \\ &=M^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

For model $f$, with $k=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^M f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^M 12\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx \\ &=\Big[3x^4-2x^6\Big]_0^M \\ &=3M^4-2M^6 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3M^4-2M^6&=3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=M$ is also the median of model $f$, so the two models have the same median.
criteria: Finds $M^2$ and integrates model 2, but does not substitute $M$, or equivalent merit

5783.stem:

Using $\text{Var}(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx-(E(X))^2$ with $E(X)=\dfrac14$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 (x^4+x^2)\,dx-\left(\dfrac14\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac15+\dfrac13\right]-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{83}{720} \end{aligned}$$

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x & 0<x<k\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $f(x)$ represents a probability density function.
State the mode of the distribution.
Find $P(X>1.5)$.

solutions.latex:
The values of $y=\dfrac{3x}{4}(2-x)$ are never negative for $0\le x\le 2$, as the graph shows.

\exfigure{1763_q25_s1}

Hence $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$.

Also
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{3}{4}\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(2^2-\dfrac{2^3}{3}\right)-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(0^2-\dfrac{0^3}{3}\right) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{54}(27x-x^3), & 0\le x\le 2.086\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

The $25^{th}$ percentile $p$ of this distribution satisfies which of the following equations?

solutions.latex:
The $25$th percentile $p$ satisfies
$$\displaystyle\int_0^p\dfrac{1}{54}(27x-x^3)\,dx=0.25$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{54}\left[\dfrac{27x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^p&=0.25 \\ \dfrac{27p^2}{2}-\dfrac{p^4}{4}&=13.5 \\ 54p^2-p^4&=54 \\ p^4-54p^2+54&=0 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

5937.stem:
The amount of time $X$ in minutes that customers spend waiting for a ride at a theme park is modelled by the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}, & 0\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$.
Find the probability that a customer waits between 2 and 4 minutes, give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.
What is the probability that a customer waits more than 4 minutes? Give answer correct to 4 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$, so
$$\int_0^5 k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_0^5=1$$
$$\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\left(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{10}-0\right)=1$$
Since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$, $\dfrac{10k}{\pi}=1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(2\le X\le 4)&=\int_2^4\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_2^4 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10}-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{10} \\ &=0.36327\ldots \\ &\approx 0.3633 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(X>4)&=\int_4^5\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_4^5 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10} \\ &=0.048943\ldots \\ &\approx 0.0489 \end{aligned}$$
